# Summary

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a final rule adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD 2026-20-09) for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes, effective November 18, 2026. The directive was prompted by reports of low clearance conditions in the right wing—between the fuel line flexible coupling and a harness support bracket clip-nut, between the fuel line flexible coupling and the hydraulic system, and between the hydraulic system and the fuel vent tube—which could create an ignition source in the fuel tank in the event of a lightning strike. The AD, based on Transport Canada AD CF-2025-49, requires operators to rectify the low clearance conditions by replacing clip-nuts and fuel tube assemblies, inspect for adequate clearance between the hydraulic lines and fuel vent tube, and perform corrective actions if problems are found. During the comment period, the FAA rejected one commenter's request to issue an emergency AD or shorten compliance times, explaining that the condition poses no fuel starvation risk and the existing timeline adequately mitigates the hazard, and also denied another commenter's request to reopen the comment period over concerns about incorporated materials and cost assumptions. The FAA estimates the directive affects 60 U.S.-registered airplanes at a cost of approximately $2,693 per aircraft ($161,580 total for U.S. operators), with potential additional on-condition repair costs of $5,772 per airplane, though some costs may be covered under the manufacturer's warranty.

# Summary of OPM Direct Final Rule on FMLA Regulations

The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations in 5 CFR Part 630 to incorporate statutory amendments enacted in January 2021 and December 2023, which will take effect December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026. The January 2021 amendments excluded certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees covered by a separate leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage, placing them instead under a VA-administered FMLA law, and clarified that annual or sick leave earned under authorities outside of title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave. The 2021 changes also broadened FMLA eligibility by making virtually all federal civilian service—including temporary or intermittent employment, as well as service with the U.S. Postal Service, Postal Regulatory Commission, and nonappropriated fund instrumentalities—count toward the 12-month qualifying service requirement. The December 2023 amendment further expanded eligibility by allowing honorable active military service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps (but not the Coast Guard or Public Health Service commissioned corps) to count toward the 12-month service requirement. Because paid parental leave (PPL) is substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, these changes also affect PPL eligibility, and the rule codifies guidance OPM previously issued through policy memoranda to agency heads in 2021 and 2024.
